title: Top 50 Decentralized Social Apps 2026: The DeSoc Index
html:
Which decentralized social apps are actually being used and built in 2026? We ranked the 50 most active decentralized and crypto social apps on four things: how many people use them, what they can do, how hard their teams are building in public on GitHub, and where they are heading. Every user number below links to its source, and every developer number comes from the projects' own public code.

How we scored the top 50 decentralized social apps

Each app gets up to 10 points in four categories, for a total out of 40.

  • Users (10): the size of the active user base, using the latest public figure. Up to 2 extra points go to unusually high engagement where the data is public. Where no active figure exists we use installs or profiles and say so.
  • Features (10): posting, video, live streaming, chat, payments, ownership and open protocols.
  • Dev activity (10): commits on the main branch of each app's public GitHub repositories between 26 July and 24 October 2026. Closed-source apps get a neutral 3, because their work cannot be checked.
  • Future (10): momentum, funding, ownership stability and product direction.

Numbers were checked on 24 and 25 October 2026. User figures move fast, so treat them as orders of magnitude.

#1 DeHub: 34/40, our top pick

DeHub is one of the early pioneers of decentralized streaming and social, first appearing on the scene in 2020. The audience is still small, but it is our top pick for the sheer development effort behind it, driven by a community using a first-of-its-kind prompt feature that lets anyone build the app in real time. It has almost every feature you will find on Twitter (X), Facebook, Twitch, Instagram and TikTok, and much more you will not, including hundreds of popular requested features that the likes of YouTube ignore, gathered from blogs all over the web.

  • Users (4/10): 5,932 accounts and 536 monthly active users. Small, but sticky: 58% of monthly users are active every week. Accounts grew 56% in the last 12 months. Live numbers: dehub.io/stats.
  • Features (10/10): Video and shorts, Live streaming, Posts, stories and DMs, Build-the-app prompts, Paid DMs, Pay-per-view, Tradable subscription NFTs, Token-gated posts, Tips, Mint uploads on-chain, Up to 90% ad revenue share, Community moderation votes, Stores and listings, Games, AI creator studio, Open source.
  • Dev activity (10/10): 6,083 public commits in 90 days across the web and mobile apps, more than any other app on this list. Contributors: 4 code authors, plus every community member who has filed a request on dehub.io/features. On DeHub, users shape the roadmap directly, so each one counts as a contributor.
  • Future (10/10): the only app here with top marks for features, dev activity and future at the same time.
Disclosure: DeHub publishes this index. Every number behind DeHub's score is public at dehub.io/stats and on GitHub.

Who is actually shipping

Users tell you where a network is today. Commits tell you where it will be next year. These are the busiest public codebases in decentralized social over the last 90 days.

The big open networks

Twelve apps on open protocols: the AT Protocol behind Bluesky, ActivityPub behind Mastodon and the fediverse, and Matrix for chat-style communities. These have the biggest audiences in decentralized social, and almost none of them pay creators.

#2 Bluesky: 33/40

Twitter-style app built on the open AT Protocol, started inside Twitter in 2019 and spun out as an independent company. Your account can move between servers and anyone can build feeds, moderation services or whole new apps on the same network.

  • Users (10/10): ~46M accounts · 10.4M monthly active · ~3M daily active. Source: Gigazine / Similarweb, Aug 2026.
  • Key features (7/10): Posts and threads, Quote posts, Custom feeds, Starter packs, Stackable moderation services, Lists, Portable accounts, Custom domain handles, DMs, Video up to 3 min, Open AT Protocol.
  • Dev activity (8/10): 978 commits in 90 days (bluesky-social/atproto + social-app).
  • Strengths: Largest audience in decentralized social by a wide margin. Custom feeds and stackable moderation are genuinely new ideas. A fast-growing ecosystem of apps (Skylight, Blacksky, Flashes) reuses the same accounts.
  • Weak spots: Active use is down roughly half from the late-2024 peak. No creator payments, tipping or subscriptions. In practice most users still sit on servers run by one company.
  • Outlook (8/10): Strong. Even if the flagship app plateaus, the protocol is becoming the default plumbing for open social, which keeps Bluesky central.
  • Website: bsky.app

#3 Matrix / Element: 33/40

Open standard for encrypted chat, with Element as the best-known app. Anyone can run a server, and servers talk to each other the way email does. Used by several European governments and many open-source projects.

  • Users (9/10): 1.15M monthly active on open federation · 190M known accounts. Source: Matrix.org Foundation annual report 2025.
  • Key features (8/10): End-to-end encrypted chat, Group rooms and spaces, Voice and video calls, Threads, Bridges to Slack, Discord, WhatsApp and more, Self-hosted servers, Federation, Bots and widgets.
  • Dev activity (8/10): 1,008 commits in 90 days (element-hq/element-web + synapse).
  • Strengths: Huge account base, real end-to-end encryption, bridges to other chat apps, and one of the most active engineering communities on this list.
  • Weak spots: It is chat rather than a public feed, so it competes more with Discord and Slack than with X. Running your own server takes real skill.
  • Outlook (8/10): Strong and steady. Government and enterprise demand for sovereign chat keeps funding flowing.
  • Website: matrix.org

#4 Mastodon: 29/40

The flagship app of the fediverse, the network of independently run servers that speak ActivityPub. Run by a German non-profit and funded by donations and sponsors.

  • Users (8/10): 826k–980k monthly active. Source: Fediverse Observer / FediDB, Jun 2026.
  • Key features (6/10): Posts with polls and media, Content warnings, Hashtag follows, Lists, Filters and mutes, Self-hosted servers, Federation with Threads and other apps, Account migration, No ads, no algorithm.
  • Dev activity (8/10): 1,134 commits in 90 days (mastodon/mastodon + mastodon-ios).
  • Strengths: Almost a million monthly users, no ads, no algorithm by default, and thousands of servers so no single owner can take it down. Very active development.
  • Weak spots: Picking a server confuses newcomers. Search and discovery are weaker than on big apps, and there is no way for creators to earn.
  • Outlook (7/10): Stable. It will not explode, but it is not going away, and its connections to Threads and Bluesky widen its reach.
  • Website: joinmastodon.org

#5 Pixelfed: 29/40

A photo-sharing app for the fediverse, often described as an open Instagram. Posts can be followed from Mastodon and other fediverse apps.

  • Users (7/10): ~105k monthly active. Source: Fediverse Observer / FediDB, Jun 2026.
  • Key features (5/10): Photo posts and albums, Stories, Collections, Filters, Hashtags and discover, Direct messages, Federation, Self-hosting, Mobile apps.
  • Dev activity (10/10): 3,726 commits in 90 days (pixelfed/pixelfed).
  • Strengths: Around 100,000 monthly users and one of the busiest codebases here, with new mobile apps shipping quickly.
  • Weak spots: Development leans heavily on one lead developer. Still far smaller than mainstream photo apps.
  • Outlook (7/10): Good. Users looking to leave Instagram have few open options, and Pixelfed is the clear leader among them.
  • Website: pixelfed.org

#10 PeerTube: 25/40

Self-hosted video platform made by French non-profit Framasoft. Each server hosts its own videos and can follow others, with peer-to-peer streaming to spread the load.

  • Users (6/10): ~50k monthly active. Source: Fediverse Observer / FediDB, Jun 2026.
  • Key features (6/10): Video hosting, Live streaming, Peer-to-peer delivery, Channels and playlists, Subtitles, Federation, Plugins and themes, Self-hosting.
  • Dev activity (7/10): 413 commits in 90 days (Chocobozzz/PeerTube).
  • Strengths: The most contributors of any video project here, live streaming built in, and no ads.
  • Weak spots: Video is expensive to host, so most servers stay small. Discovery across servers is limited.
  • Outlook (6/10): Steady. Popular with schools, public bodies and creators who want their own home for video.
  • Website: joinpeertube.org

#14 Misskey: 23/40

A fediverse microblogging app from Japan with emoji reactions, drive storage and lots of customization.

  • Users (6/10): misskey.io 450k+ registered (Feb 2024). Source: Wikipedia.
  • Key features (6/10): Posts, Emoji reactions, Custom emoji, Drive file storage, Channels, Antennas (keyword feeds), Plugins and widgets, Federation.
  • Dev activity (5/10): 175 commits in 90 days (misskey-dev/misskey).
  • Strengths: Huge in Japan, with misskey.io past 450,000 accounts in 2024. Active development and a lively culture.
  • Weak spots: Mostly Japanese-speaking, so growth outside Japan is slow.
  • Outlook (6/10): Solid in its home market.
  • Website: misskey-hub.net

#17 Bridgy Fed: 21/40

A bridge that lets Mastodon, Bluesky and personal websites follow and reply to each other.

  • Users (4/10): Not published. Source: Not published.
  • Key features (4/10): Bridges Mastodon and Bluesky, Bridges personal websites, Follow across networks, Replies and likes across networks, Opt-in by design.
  • Dev activity (7/10): 486 commits in 90 days (snarfed/bridgy-fed).
  • Strengths: Makes the open networks feel like one. Very active for a small team.
  • Weak spots: Users have to opt in, and it depends on the goodwill of the networks it connects.
  • Outlook (6/10): Important plumbing. Grows as the networks it bridges grow.
  • Website: fed.brid.gy

#18 Friendica: 21/40

One of the oldest fediverse apps, closer to Facebook than Twitter, with long posts, groups and events.

  • Users (3/10): Small, not published. Source: Not published.
  • Key features (6/10): Long posts, Groups, Events, Photo albums, Private posts, Federation with Mastodon and Diaspora, Self-hosting.
  • Dev activity (8/10): 945 commits in 90 days (friendica/friendica).
  • Strengths: Very active volunteer team for its size and connects to almost every other fediverse network.
  • Weak spots: Small user base and an older-looking interface.
  • Outlook (4/10): Stable niche.
  • Website: friendi.ca

#20 Skylight: 20/40

A short-video app built on the AT Protocol, backed by Mark Cuban.

  • Users (6/10): 380k users · ~95k monthly active (Jan 2026). Source: TechCrunch, Jan 2026.
  • Key features (5/10): Short video, Editor and effects, Curators, Bluesky login, Custom feeds, Comments.
  • Dev activity (3/10): Closed source.
  • Strengths: Jumped to 380,000 users in January 2026 when TikTok's US deal closed. Uses Bluesky accounts.
  • Weak spots: Monthly users were about 95,000, so many sign-ups did not stay.
  • Outlook (6/10): Good. Video on an open network is a real gap.
  • Website: skylight.social

#23 Blacksky: 20/40

Independent infrastructure and a community on the AT Protocol, built by and for Black users of Bluesky.

  • Users (3/10): Not published. Source: Not published.
  • Key features (5/10): Own personal data servers, Community moderation, Custom feeds, Bluesky-compatible, Community app.
  • Dev activity (6/10): 332 commits in 90 days (blacksky-algorithms/rsky).
  • Strengths: Runs its own servers and moderation, proving the AT Protocol can work without Bluesky the company.
  • Weak spots: Small, focused community.
  • Outlook (6/10): Good. A model for other communities that want to own their corner of the network.
  • Website: blacksky.community

#24 Lemmy: 19/40

A federated link-sharing and discussion site, like an open Reddit. Boomed during the 2023 Reddit API protest.

  • Users (6/10): ~35k–43k monthly active. Source: Fediverse Observer / FediDB, Jun 2026.
  • Key features (4/10): Communities, Up and down votes, Threaded comments, Moderation tools, Federation, Self-hosting, Mobile clients.
  • Dev activity (4/10): 54 commits in 90 days (LemmyNet/lemmy).
  • Strengths: Around 40,000 monthly users across many servers and a familiar community-and-vote format.
  • Weak spots: Growth has flattened since 2023 and development has slowed.
  • Outlook (5/10): Steady. Benefits each time Reddit upsets its users.
  • Website: join-lemmy.org

#27 Bonfire: 19/40

A modular fediverse app where communities pick the features they want, such as circles for private sharing or custom feeds.

  • Users (2/10): Early stage. Source: Not published.
  • Key features (6/10): Custom feeds, Circles for private sharing, Boundaries per post, Extensions, Federation, Self-hosting.
  • Dev activity (6/10): 355 commits in 90 days (bonfire-networks/bonfire-app).
  • Strengths: Very flexible and steadily developed by an active team.
  • Weak spots: Still early, with few users.
  • Outlook (5/10): Promising for communities that want more control than Mastodon offers.
  • Website: bonfirenetworks.org

Nostr and Bitcoin social

Nostr is a simple protocol where your identity is a key pair and your posts travel through relays anyone can run. Most of these apps pay creators in bitcoin through Lightning "zaps". The audience is small, about 15,000 trusted monthly users in late 2025, but the builders are some of the busiest in the space.

#6 Amethyst: 28/40

The most feature-rich Nostr app for Android. Nostr is a simple protocol where your identity is a key pair and posts are sent through relays anyone can run.

  • Users (4/10): 100k+ Android installs. Source: Google Play.
  • Key features (8/10): Nostr posts and replies, Zaps (Lightning tips), Communities, Live streams, Marketplace listings, Private DMs, Long-form articles, Polls, Multiple accounts, Tor support.
  • Dev activity (10/10): 4,275 commits in 90 days (vitorpamplona/amethyst).
  • Strengths: Packs in communities, live streams, a marketplace, private messages and Lightning tips. The second most active public codebase on this list.
  • Weak spots: Android only, and the wider Nostr network is still small, with roughly 15,000 trusted monthly users.
  • Outlook (6/10): Good for builders and Bitcoin fans. Growth depends on Nostr as a whole reaching more people.
  • Website: github.com/vitorpamplona/amethyst

#13 Damus: 24/40

The first major Nostr app for iPhone, now joined by Notedeck, a desktop client from the same team.

  • Users (4/10): Not disclosed (iOS-first). Source: Nostr statistics, Oct 2025.
  • Key features (6/10): Nostr posts, Zaps, Encrypted DMs, Long-form reads, Relay control, Notedeck desktop app, Multiple accounts.
  • Dev activity (8/10): 1,481 commits in 90 days (damus-io/damus + notedeck).
  • Strengths: Simple, well-known brand in Nostr, built-in Lightning tips, and very active work on Notedeck.
  • Weak spots: Apple's rules on tipping have caused friction before. User numbers are not published.
  • Outlook (6/10): Good within Nostr. Notedeck could make it the main desktop home for the protocol.
  • Website: damus.io

#22 Primal: 20/40

A fast, polished Nostr app on iOS, Android and web with a built-in Bitcoin Lightning wallet.

  • Users (4/10): 50k+ Android installs · Nostr has ~14.8k monthly active trusted users. Source: Google Play.
  • Key features (7/10): Nostr feeds, Built-in Lightning wallet, Zaps, Trending and explore, Long-form reads, Media hosting, Premium accounts.
  • Dev activity (3/10): 39 commits in 90 days (PrimalHQ android + ios + web).
  • Strengths: Probably the easiest way into Nostr, with smooth feeds and tips.
  • Weak spots: Nostr's total audience is small, around 15,000 trusted monthly users in late 2025.
  • Outlook (6/10): Good if Nostr grows. Primal is best placed to catch new users.
  • Website: primal.net

#25 Fountain: 19/40

A podcast and music app that pays listeners and creators in bitcoin, with social features on Nostr.

  • Users (5/10): 100k+ Android installs. Source: Google Play.
  • Key features (6/10): Podcasts, Music, Bitcoin rewards for listening, Clips, Comments on Nostr, Creator payouts.
  • Dev activity (3/10): Closed source.
  • Strengths: More than 100,000 Android installs and real payments to creators.
  • Weak spots: Low store ratings and closed source.
  • Outlook (5/10): Good niche in podcasting.
  • Website: fountain.fm

#30 Stacker News: 18/40

A Hacker News-style forum where every upvote sends real bitcoin to the poster.

  • Users (3/10): Small community. Source: Not published.
  • Key features (5/10): Posts and links, Sats rewards for upvotes, Territories, Bounties, Jobs board, Lightning wallet login.
  • Dev activity (5/10): 117 commits in 90 days (stackernews/stacker.news).
  • Strengths: Proves micropayments for content can work. Good discussion quality.
  • Weak spots: Small, mostly Bitcoin-focused audience.
  • Outlook (5/10): Steady niche.
  • Website: stacker.news

#34 noStrudel: 17/40

A power-user Nostr web client built by one developer.

  • Users (3/10): Not disclosed. Source: Not published.
  • Key features (5/10): Power-user Nostr feeds, Streams, Lists, Relay tools, Many NIPs supported.
  • Dev activity (5/10): 135 commits in 90 days (hzrd149/nostrudel).
  • Strengths: Ships constantly and has many tools.
  • Weak spots: Not aimed at beginners.
  • Outlook (4/10): Steady niche.
  • Website: nostrudel.ninja

#39 Coracle: 16/40

A Nostr web client focused on groups and choosing relays.

  • Users (3/10): Not disclosed. Source: Not published.
  • Key features (5/10): Feeds, Groups, Relay controls, Web of trust filtering.
  • Dev activity (4/10): 76 commits in 90 days (coracle-social/coracle).
  • Strengths: Good for communities.
  • Weak spots: Small audience.
  • Outlook (4/10): Niche.
  • Website: coracle.social

#40 Iris: 16/40

A simple, fast Nostr web client.

  • Users (3/10): Not disclosed. Source: Not published.
  • Key features (4/10): Feeds, Chat, Media, Fast web app.
  • Dev activity (5/10): 156 commits in 90 days (irislib/iris-client).
  • Strengths: Easy to start with.
  • Weak spots: Small audience.
  • Outlook (4/10): Niche.
  • Website: iris.to

#43 zap.stream: 15/40

Live streaming over Nostr, paid in bitcoin tips.

  • Users (3/10): Not disclosed. Source: Not published.
  • Key features (5/10): Live streams, Zaps, Live chat, Stream clips.
  • Dev activity (3/10): 12 commits in 90 days (v0l/zap.stream).
  • Strengths: Real-time Lightning payments.
  • Weak spots: Small streamer base.
  • Outlook (4/10): Niche but useful.
  • Website: zap.stream

#45 Snort: 14/40

A long-standing Nostr web client.

  • Users (3/10): Not disclosed. Source: Not published.
  • Key features (4/10): Feeds, Zaps, DMs, Web app.
  • Dev activity (4/10): 74 commits in 90 days (v0l/snort).
  • Strengths: Familiar, steady.
  • Weak spots: Small audience.
  • Outlook (3/10): Niche.
  • Website: snort.social

#49 YakiHonne: 11/40

A Nostr app for long-form posts and curated collections.

  • Users (2/10): Not disclosed. Source: Not published.
  • Key features (5/10): Long-form posts, Curations, Zaps, Videos, Mobile app.
  • Dev activity (1/10): 0 commits in 90 days (YakiHonne web + mobile).
  • Strengths: Good long-form tools.
  • Weak spots: Public repos quiet since October 2025.
  • Outlook (3/10): Weak.
  • Website: yakihonne.com

Crypto social and SocialFi

Apps that put tokens, coins or on-chain ownership at the centre. This is where 2026 hit hardest: two protocols changed owners, a hack drained one app, and creator coins drew heavy criticism.

#8 Audius: 26/40

A music streaming platform where artists upload directly and fans stream for free. Now runs on Solana and launched artist coins in 2025.

  • Users (8/10): Up to 8M monthly active (claimed, 2025). Source: Solana Compass, 2025.
  • Key features (7/10): Music uploads, Free streaming, Playlists, Artist coins, Gated tracks, Remix contests, Comments, Developer API, Mobile apps.
  • Dev activity (5/10): 129 commits in 90 days (AudiusProject/apps).
  • Strengths: Big catalogue, well-known artists, and a real music business through deals such as Friends & Family.
  • Weak spots: The 8 million monthly user figure is a company claim from 2025 and active use has likely fallen since. It suffered a $6M governance exploit in 2022.
  • Outlook (6/10): Decent. Artist coins and label partnerships give it a clear model if fans follow.
  • Website: audius.co

#9 Hive: 26/40

A blockchain built for social content, created in 2020 when the community split from Steem. Many front ends sit on top, including PeakD and Ecency, plus games such as Splinterlands.

  • Users (5/10): Monthly actives down 8% in Feb 2026 · Ecency 50k+ installs. Source: Hive Statistics (arcange), Feb 2026.
  • Key features (7/10): Long-form blog posts, Upvote rewards, Curation rewards, Communities, Many front ends (PeakD, Ecency), Free, fast transactions, Games, Built-in DEX, Short video (3Speak).
  • Dev activity (9/10): 1,780 commits in 90 days (ecency/vision-next; Hive core is on GitLab).
  • Strengths: Free transactions, rewards for posting and curating, and a loyal community. Ecency alone shipped more than 1,700 commits in 90 days.
  • Weak spots: Monthly active users have been drifting down. Rewards can encourage low-quality posting, and new users find it complex.
  • Outlook (5/10): Mixed. Strong builders, but it needs a hit app to bring in new people.
  • Website: hive.io

#15 Farcaster: 22/40

A crypto-native social protocol with its own app (formerly Warpcast). Known for mini apps inside posts, built-in wallets and token launches.

  • Users (7/10): <250k monthly active · <60k daily active. Source: KuCoin News, Oct 2026.
  • Key features (8/10): Casts and replies, Channels, Mini apps (Frames), Built-in wallet, Tipping, Token launches, Direct casts, Developer API (Neynar).
  • Dev activity (3/10): 44 commits in 90 days (farcasterxyz/snapchain + hub-monorepo).
  • Strengths: Rich features, a builder-heavy crowd and deep wallet integration. Still one of the most visible crypto social networks.
  • Weak spots: Founders sold it to Neynar in January 2026 and the $180M raised went back to investors. In October it passed to Network School. Revenue collapsed from about $28M in Q1 to $246k in Q3 2026.
  • Outlook (4/10): Weak for now. Another change of owner in nine months is a hard reset.
  • Website: farcaster.xyz

#16 Base App: 22/40

Coinbase's wallet, relaunched in July 2025 as an all-in-one app combining a social feed (built on Farcaster), chat, creator coins and trading.

  • Users (6/10): Not disclosed. Source: The Defiant, Jan 2026.
  • Key features (7/10): Smart wallet, Social feed on Farcaster, Creator coins, Mini apps, Chat, Trading, Payments, Onramp from Coinbase.

What is the biggest decentralized social network in 2026?

Bluesky, with about 46 million accounts and roughly 10 million monthly active users. Matrix is bigger by accounts but is a chat network. Mastodon leads the fediverse with close to a million monthly users.

Which decentralized social apps pay creators?

DeHub, Audius, Zora, Hive, Paragraph, Fountain and Stacker News all pay creators natively. Bluesky and Mastodon do not.

Why is DeHub ranked #1 if its user base is small?

Because of the development effort. DeHub has been building decentralized streaming and social since 2020, its community can build the app in real time with a prompt feature, and it shipped more public code in the last 90 days than any other app here. Its audience is still small, which is why it scores 4/10 on users, but it is the only app with top marks on features, dev activity and future.

How was GitHub activity measured?

We cloned each project's main public repositories and counted commits on the default branch between 26 July and 24 October 2026. Closed-source apps get a neutral 3/10.

Is decentralized social media safe to use?

The established apps here are real, working networks, many of them open source. Token rewards carry market risk, so never treat crypto earnings as guaranteed income. For a deeper comparison of the biggest platforms, read our guide to the best decentralised social media platforms.

Which decentralized social apps are actually being used and built in 2026? We ranked the 50 most active decentralized and crypto social apps on four things: **how many people use them, what they can do, how hard their teams are building in public on GitHub, and where they are heading**. Every user number below links to its source, and every developer number comes from the projects' own public code.

![The DeSoc Index 2026: how we scored 50 decentralized social apps](/media/fig-desoc-method.jpg)

## How we scored the top 50 decentralized social apps

Each app gets up to 10 points in four categories, for a total out of 40.

- **Users (10):** the size of the active user base, using the latest public figure. Up to 2 extra points go to unusually high engagement where the data is public. Where no active figure exists we use installs or profiles and say so.
- **Features (10):** posting, video, live streaming, chat, payments, ownership and open protocols.
- **Dev activity (10):** commits on the main branch of each app's public GitHub repositories between 26 July and 24 October 2026. Closed-source apps get a neutral 3, because their work cannot be checked.
- **Future (10):** momentum, funding, ownership stability and product direction.

Numbers were checked on 24 and 25 October 2026. User figures move fast, so treat them as orders of magnitude.

## #1 DeHub: 34/40, our top pick

![DeHub, built in public: 6,083 commits in 90 days, the most of any decentralized social app](/media/fig-desoc-dehub.jpg)

DeHub is one of the early pioneers of decentralized streaming and social, first appearing on the scene in 2020. The audience is still small, but it is our top pick for the sheer development effort behind it, driven by a community using a first-of-its-kind prompt feature that lets anyone build the app in real time. It has almost every feature you will find on Twitter (X), Facebook, Twitch, Instagram and TikTok, and much more you will not, including hundreds of popular requested features that the likes of YouTube ignore, gathered from blogs all over the web.

- **Users (4/10):** 5,932 accounts and 536 monthly active users. Small, but sticky: 58% of monthly users are active every week. Accounts grew 56% in the last 12 months. Live numbers: [dehub.io/stats](https://dehub.io/stats).
- **Features (10/10):** Video and shorts, Live streaming, Posts, stories and DMs, Build-the-app prompts, Paid DMs, Pay-per-view, Tradable subscription NFTs, Token-gated posts, Tips, Mint uploads on-chain, Up to 90% ad revenue share, Community moderation votes, Stores and listings, Games, AI creator studio, Open source.
- **Dev activity (10/10):** 6,083 public commits in 90 days across the web and mobile apps, more than any other app on this list. Contributors: 4 code authors, plus every community member who has filed a request on [dehub.io/features](https://dehub.io/features). On DeHub, users shape the roadmap directly, so each one counts as a contributor.
- **Future (10/10):** the only app here with top marks for features, dev activity and future at the same time.

> Disclosure: DeHub publishes this index. Every number behind DeHub's score is public at dehub.io/stats and on GitHub.

## Who is actually shipping

Users tell you where a network is today. Commits tell you where it will be next year. These are the busiest public codebases in decentralized social over the last 90 days.

Twelve apps on open protocols: the AT Protocol behind Bluesky, ActivityPub behind Mastodon and the fediverse, and Matrix for chat-style communities. These have the biggest audiences in decentralized social, and almost none of them pay creators.

### #2 Bluesky: 33/40

Twitter-style app built on the open AT Protocol, started inside Twitter in 2019 and spun out as an independent company. Your account can move between servers and anyone can build feeds, moderation services or whole new apps on the same network.

- **Users (10/10):** ~46M accounts · 10.4M monthly active · ~3M daily active. Source: [Gigazine / Similarweb, Aug 2026](https://gigazine.net/gsc_news/en/20260812-blueskys-active-user/).

- **Dev activity (8/10):** 978 commits in 90 days (bluesky-social/atproto + social-app).
- **Strengths:** Largest audience in decentralized social by a wide margin. Custom feeds and stackable moderation are genuinely new ideas. A fast-growing ecosystem of apps (Skylight, Blacksky, Flashes) reuses the same accounts.
- **Weak spots:** Active use is down roughly half from the late-2024 peak. No creator payments, tipping or subscriptions. In practice most users still sit on servers run by one company.
- **Outlook (8/10):** Strong. Even if the flagship app plateaus, the protocol is becoming the default plumbing for open social, which keeps Bluesky central.
- **Website:** [bsky.app](https://bsky.app)

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the biggest decentralized social network in 2026?

Bluesky, with about 46 million accounts and roughly 10 million monthly active users. Matrix is bigger by accounts but is a chat network. Mastodon leads the fediverse with close to a million monthly users.

### Which decentralized social apps pay creators?

DeHub, Audius, Zora, Hive, Paragraph, Fountain and Stacker News all pay creators natively. Bluesky and Mastodon do not.

### Why is DeHub ranked #1 if its user base is small?

Because of the development effort. DeHub has been building decentralized streaming and social since 2020, its community can build the app in real time with a prompt feature, and it shipped more public code in the last 90 days than any other app here. Its audience is still small, which is why it scores 4/10 on users, but it is the only app with top marks on features, dev activity and future.

### How was GitHub activity measured?

We cloned each project's main public repositories and counted commits on the default branch between 26 July and 24 October 2026. Closed-source apps get a neutral 3/10.

### Is decentralized social media safe to use?

The established apps here are real, working networks, many of them open source. Token rewards carry market risk, so never treat crypto earnings as guaranteed income.
